# Writing a Report {#sec-writing-reports}

Almost everything you produce in a working life ends up inside a document someone else
reads.  The analysis might be excellent, but if the report is confusing, or buries the
answer on page four, or presents a number without saying what it means, the work does not
land.  This chapter is about the document.

The advice here is the same whether you are writing the course project, a memo for a farm
manager, or a report for a client -- only the length changes.  You now have charts worth
putting in one, and this is where they go.

## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

::: {.objectives}
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- Structure a report so a reader finds the answer quickly
- Write an opening that states what you found, rather than what you did
- Present a number so that it means something to the reader
- Introduce a chart in the text rather than leaving it to speak for itself
- Say what your analysis cannot tell you, without undermining it
:::

## Lead With the Answer {#sec-lead-with-answer}

The commonest mistake in a data report is telling the story in the order you did the work:
here is the data, here is how I cleaned it, here is the method, here is the result, and
finally -- on the last page -- here is what it means.  That is the order of your effort, not
the order of your reader's interest.

Your reader wants the answer.  Put it first, in plain language, in the opening paragraph:

> Canola yields in the black soil zone averaged 42 bushels per acre over the last five
> years, about 15% higher than in the brown zone.  The gap is consistent across every year
> in the data, so it is unlikely to be weather in any single season.

That is a whole report in three sentences.  Everything that follows is there so a reader who
wants to check the claim can do so -- but a reader who only has thirty seconds still leaves
with the finding.

Write this paragraph last, once you know what you actually found.

## A Structure That Works {#sec-report-structure}

Almost any data report fits this shape.  For a short piece, each numbered item is a
paragraph; for a long one, a section.

1. **The answer.**  What you found, stated plainly.  As above.
2. **The question.**  What were you asked, and why does it matter?  A reader needs to know
   what problem this is solving before they will care about the method.
3. **The data.**  Where it came from, what it covers, and what it does *not* cover.  If you
   cleaned or filtered it, say what you dropped and why -- this is where a reader decides
   whether to trust the rest.
4. **What you did.**  In plain language.  Not every function you called; the idea of the
   analysis.  "We compared the average yield in each soil zone, weighting by acres so that
   larger regions counted more."
5. **The results.**  The main body: charts, tables, and the numbers that matter, each one
   introduced in the text.
6. **What it means, and what it does not.**  The interpretation, and the honest caveats.
7. **Sources.**  Where the data came from, so someone else could repeat the work.

Two things about the order.  The answer comes first and the caveats come last, which is the
opposite of how nervous writers do it -- they hedge for two pages before committing to
anything.  Hedge at the end, once the reader knows what you are hedging about.

## Presenting Numbers {#sec-presenting-numbers}

A number on its own means very little.  `42.3851` is a calculation result, not yet an answer.

**Round to what you can defend.**  If your yields are measured to the nearest tenth of a
bushel, reporting `42.3851` implies a precision you do not have.  Write 42.4, or often just
42.  Decimals that carry no information make a report harder to read and make the writer
look like they pasted a cell without thinking.

**Give the number a comparison.**  "Average yield was 42 bu/ac" is a fact.  "Average yield
was 42 bu/ac, about 15% above the provincial average" is a finding.  A reader almost never
knows whether a number is high or low on its own -- give them something to measure it
against, whether that is another group, another year, or a target.

**Say the units, every time.**  Bushels per acre and pounds per acre are both "yield", and
we have already seen what happens when they get mixed.

**Do not report more numbers than you can discuss.**  A table of forty figures where you
comment on three is forty figures of noise.  Cut it to the three, or move the rest to an
appendix.

## Charts in a Report {#sec-charts-in-reports}

A chart in a report needs three things beyond the chart itself: a number, a caption, and a
sentence in the text that says what to look at.

Introduce every chart before the reader reaches it -- "Figure 3 shows average yield by soil
zone" -- and then say what it shows: "the black zone is consistently higher, and the gap
does not close in the drought year."  A chart dropped into a page with no introduction makes
the reader do work you should have done for them, and different readers will take away
different things.

The rule of thumb is one chart, one point.  If you cannot say in a single sentence what a
chart shows, it is probably doing two jobs and should be two charts.

## Saying What You Do Not Know {#sec-caveats}

Students often think admitting a limitation weakens the report.  In my experience the
analyst who names the weaknesses of their own work is the one you end up trusting, because
you know they are not hiding anything you might find later.

The caveats worth stating are the ones that would change a reader's decision:

- **What the data does not cover.**  Insured acres only.  One province.  Five years, one of
  them a drought.
- **What you assumed.**  That the sample is representative.  That a variety planted in two
  zones performs comparably.
- **What you could not separate.**  If high-yielding varieties are also grown on the best
  land, your data cannot tell you which is responsible.

Say these plainly, in a sentence each, and then stop.  A report that spends a page
apologising for itself is as unhelpful as one that admits nothing.

## The Course Project {#sec-project-report}

The course project is a report of exactly this kind: a question about agricultural data, an
analysis you carry out yourself, and a written argument about what you found.  The structure
above is the one to follow.

Marks do not go to the most complicated analysis.  A straightforward comparison, clearly
explained, with honest caveats and a chart that makes its point, will beat an elaborate model
the reader cannot follow.
